cards.explanation: The answer is twilight, that dim stretch when the day winds down. The LORD says to offer one lamb in the morning and the other at twilight (Numbers 28:4). So the day gets an offering at each end, with the same grain offering and drink offering both times (Numbers 28:8). Very organized, and I respect a good schedule.

The answer is True, every day. The LORD calls this pair of lambs a regular burnt offering "each day" (Numbers 28:3). Feast days get their own offerings later, but those are added on top. The daily pair is the steady rhythm underneath it all, steady like my oven timer, which has never once asked for a day off.

The answer is Sinai. Numbers 28:6 says this regular burnt offering was "…established at Mount Sinai…" So it's been around since Sinai and is not something brand new. Some things have a long history. Mine starts with a 25 cent price sticker in a bakery bin.

The answer is False, because nothing gets replaced. The Sabbath offering is "…in addition to the regular burnt offering and its drink offering." (Numbers 28:10). So a Sabbath has the morning lamb, the twilight lamb and the two Sabbath lambs. That's four lambs by my count, and I counted twice on my mustache to be sure.

The answer is at each new moon. Numbers 28:11 puts this offering at "…the beginning of every month…" and Numbers 28:14 says it's made "…at each new moon throughout the year." So the month starts with a big offering. Look up at the night sky and you've got a calendar.

The answer is goat. Numbers 28:15 says one male goat is presented to the LORD as a sin offering. It comes in addition to the regular burnt offering with its drink offering. So the goat has its own job apart from the bulls, the ram and the lambs.

The answer is unleavened bread, the whole week. Numbers 28:17 says the feast is on the fifteenth day, and "for seven days unleavened bread is to be eaten." Unleavened means bread made without leaven. As a cookie man, I respect any dough that doesn't rise.

The answer is True. Numbers 28:18 says, "On the first day there is to be a sacred assembly; you must not do any regular work." So the feast opens with a sacred assembly and the regular work put down. A whole day off from regular work? I'd need a lie-down just thinking about a day away from my ovens.

The answer is another sacred assembly. Numbers 28:25 says, "On the seventh day you shall hold a sacred assembly; you must not do any regular work." The first day opens with one, and the seventh day has one too. That's a lot of gathering for one feast.

The answer is grain, friends! Numbers 28:26 says, "On the day of firstfruits, when you present an offering of new grain to the LORD during the Feast of Weeks…" As a cookie guy, I respect anything that starts with new grain. The day also comes with a sacred assembly and no regular work, so that's a day off AND an offering of new grain. Nice.

The answer is trumpets, friends. Numbers 29:1 says, "This will be a day for you to sound the trumpets." It's a sacred assembly on the first day of the seventh month, and it comes with a sound you can hear. That's one day nobody could call quiet.

The answer is False, because it stacks. Numbers 29:6 says, "These are in addition to the monthly and daily burnt offerings with their prescribed grain offerings and drink offerings." So the first day of the seventh month gets its own offering on top of the others. That's a day I'd need three extra timers just to read about.
The answer is humble. Numbers 29:7 says, "…you shall humble yourselves; you must not do any work." The text doesn't spell out how, so I won't guess. It does say there's a sacred assembly that day.

The answer is seven days, friends! Numbers 29:12 says, "…you shall observe a feast to the LORD for seven days." That matches the feast after Passover (Numbers 28:17). Seven whole days of feasting is a party I'd need extra cookie boxes for. Hold onto that thought, because verse 35 has one more day waiting at the end.

The answer is False. Numbers 29:35 says, "On the eighth day you are to hold a solemn assembly; you must not do any regular work." So Israel finishes the seven days of feast, figures it's back to work, and the eighth day is still waiting. I'd take that deal every time. On that eighth day, the regular work waits.

The answer is their vow and freewill offerings. Numbers 29:39 says these scheduled offerings are "…in addition to your vow and freewill offerings…" So the calendar doesn't use up what people want to bring on their own. That's a nice thing to leave room for.

The answer is True. Numbers 29:40 says, "So Moses spoke all this to the Israelites just as the LORD had commanded him." Moses, Israel's leader, passes it on just as he was told. Nothing added and nothing trimmed, and that's how I like my recipes.
